Fertilised eggs of the lion scallop Nodipecten subnodosus contain an energy content of 2.12 × 10⁻³ joules , a value derived from the measured egg diameter of 52.5 micrometres and applied allometric relationships for dry weight from related pectinid species. In laboratory cultures maintained at 26.5 °C [T = 26.5 °C], trochophore larvae hatch and transition into D-stage veligers approximately 1 day [ab = approximately 1 day] after fertilisation. At this point of first exogenous feeding, the newly formed prodissoconch shell measures 0.006 centimetres [Lb = 0.006 centimetres], representing the mean of the reported size range for the onset of planktotrophic feeding in pectinid larvae. The corresponding dry weight at birth was determined through linear regression of larval shell length and dry weight over the entire 35-day rearing period, yielding a value of 2.3398 × 10⁻⁸ g rams at a temperature of 26.5 °C [T = 26.5 °C]. These early life-history parameters, measured under controlled temperature conditions, provide a baseline for understanding the species' high fecundity and rapid early growth.

During the larval phase at a constant temperature of 26.5 °C [T = 26.5 °C], the pediveliger stage attains competency for metamorphosis after approximately 14 days  post-hatching. The shell length at the onset of metamorphosis was recorded at 0.0210 centimetres , with the actual transition spanning a size window of 200 to 400 micrometres. At the conclusion of the metamorphic period, the dry weight of newly settled juveniles was measured at 1.68169 × 10⁻⁷ g rams, derived from the same larval growth regression at a temperature of 26.5 °C [T = 26.5 °C]. This metamorphic transition involves a substantial body plan reorganisation, including velum loss and gill development, after which the post-larval mollusc begins its benthic existence. The relatively short pre-metamorphic period and small size at settlement are consistent with observations in other fast-growing pectinid species inhabiting warm temperate waters.

Sexual maturation in Nodipecten subnodosus occurs at a shell length of 6.6 centimetres [Lp = 6.6 centimetres], defined as the size at which 50% of individuals exhibit active gametogenesis. This milestone is reached approximately 406 days [tp = approximately 406 days] after hatching, under the integrated thermal conditions of a two-phase cultivat at a temperature of 23.8 °C [T = 23.8 °C]ion experiment. The first phase took place in the laboratory at 24 °C until scallops reached 2 mm in length, followed by a field deployment in Bahia Loreto where surface water temperatures averaged 23.80 °C [T = 23.80 °C] over the remainder of the 406-day period. At this point, the wet total weight of the gonad-bearing tissue is 25.34 grams [Wwp = 25.34 grams], calculated from length-weight and meat-weight regressions. This size at puberty is relatively large compared to other commercially exploited pectinids, suggesting that the lion scallop delays reproductive investment until a substantial somatic frame is established.

The maximum asymptotic shell length for this population from Bahia Los Angeles, derived from von Bertalanffy growth models fitted to random monthly samples collected from January to December 2006, is 19 centimetres [Li = 19 centimetres]. The corresponding ultimate wet total weight was estimated at 513.5 grams [Wwi = 513.5 grams] using the established length-total weight relationship (TW = 0.2979 × L²·⁹¹⁹³). Field surveys indicate that a large, fully grown female can release an average of 84,247 eggs per day  during the spawning season at 20 °C [T = 20 °C], a rate derived from laboratory-induced spawning events and an assumption of approximately 1.5 major spawning events per year. This high daily reproductive output, combined with the extended spawning period typical of the species, results in a lifetime fecundity that likely numbers in the tens of millions.

Maximum longevity in the lion scallop has been estimated at approximately 7 years [am = approximately 7 years] under the prevailing thermal regime of 23 °C [T = 23 °C], based on growth record analyses from natural populations. This lifespan, while moderate among pectinids, allows for multiple reproductive seasons and a cumulative fecundity that supports the species' role as a dominant filter feeder in its coastal ecosystem. The relatively large ultimate body size and slow attainment of puberty are balanced by an extraordinarily high instantaneous fecundity at large body sizes, a life-history strategy that appears well suited to the variable upwelling conditions of the Gulf of California. Comparisons with congeners suggest that N. subnodosus stands out for its combination of high fecundity and substantial adult mass, traits that have made it a target for both wild fisheries and aquaculture development throughout its range.
